newsitem.title: USA: FORECAST - East Europe bourses see growth slowing.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - East Europe bourses see growth slowing.

text.p: Investors in some Eastern European stock exchanges have seen prices surge this year, but the rapid pace is unlikely to be maintained, leading market officials said on Monday.
Prices in Hungary and Poland have risen 80 percent in the past year, while Russian stock prices have more than doubled.

"All of these stock markets are relatively new on the emerging markets scene but in their relatively short history they have grown enormously," Robert Shakotko, manager of the International Finance Corporation's (IFC) emerging markets database, told a press seminar.
The IFC, the private sector arm of the World Bank, on Monday launched three new daily global indices, tracking stock prices in Morocco, Egypt and Eastern Europe's giant -- Russia.
The 25 stocks in the Russian index have risen more 128 percent since the beginning of the year.
However, Jozsef Rotyis, chairman of the Budapest Stock Exchange, said this rapid growth was unlikely to continue.
"Emerging markets, not only the securities, but the markets themselves, tend to be very volatile," he said. "I'm not very sure if we can sustain this spectacular growth."
However, he was confident the market would continue to develop if companies remained profitable.
Lech Biegunski, board member of the Warsaw Stock Exchange, said the market had returned to normal this year after two years of low volume.
Another reason for the rise in prices was the improvement in management standards in Polish firms.
"Because of that I expect a constant growth of the index in the coming years," he said.
Cesare Calari, manager of the IFC's capital markets division, said a "wall of worry" had replaced the Berlin Wall for investors and regulators in Eastern Europe.
Political uncertainty linked with the health problems of President Boris Yeltsin, who is awaiting heart surgery, drove Russian prices sharply lower earlier this month.
However, representatives of some of Russia's neighbours did not believe this uncertainty would affect their markets.
Rotyis said any dramatic events in Russia could have a short-term impact on all markets.
"As we are economically and politically independent, I do not see, even in the worst case scenario, any long-term effect on the development of our markets," he said.
Biegunsky said investor interest in Russia could benefit the whole region "I do not think that should in any way diminish interest in other markets in the region.
